issues.display_title: Issue #172: Reduce Ram Usage on Stitching Feature
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

Description

The Stitching feature (merging multiple photos into a 360 panorama) uses a large amount of RAM while processing, especially with high-resolution source photos or when several images are combined at once. On computers with limited memory (8-16GB), this can slow the whole app down, cause it to freeze, or crash entirely — forcing the user to restart and redo the stitch.

This gets worse as photo resolution and photo count increase, so it's currently a bigger risk for users doing high-quality panorama shoots. Goal: bring RAM usage down so stitching completes reliably without freezing/crashing, even on lower-spec machines.

issues.display_title: Issue #183: Switch product analytics from Aptabase to self-hosted Countly
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

Description

Problem: We have no idea how the app is actually being used. The app was supposed to report usage to Aptabase, but the reporting was never actually finished — every event the app tried to send went nowhere. So the analytics dashboard has always been empty, and we've been guessing about which features matter to users.

Solution: Point analytics at our own Countly server (data.gothru.org) instead, and actually finish the wiring so events really get sent.

Countly is self-hosted, so usage data stays on our own server instead of a third party's.

What gets reported:

  • App opens and closes — how many people use the app, how often they come back, and how long a session lasts.
  • Basic environment — operating system and app version, so we can see who's still on an old build.
  • The actions already wired up in the app — switching viewers, changing theme or language, file operations (rename, copy, move, delete, create folder), sorting, bookmarks, uploads, GPS updates, orientation fixes, and app updates.

What is NOT reported: no file names, no folder paths, no image contents, no account details. Each install is identified only by a random ID generated on that machine — it can't be traced back to a person.

Behavior:

  • Only released builds report. Running the app locally during development stays silent, so our own testing doesn't pollute real usage numbers.
  • Analytics never interrupts the user. If the server is unreachable or slow, the app carries on as normal — nothing is shown, nothing is blocked, nothing fails.
  • Closing the app sends one final "session ended" note. If the server doesn't answer, the app waits at most 2 seconds and quits anyway.

Also fixed along the way:

  • Some actions were reporting the same thing under three different spellings, which split one number into three in the dashboard and made it unreadable. Now unified.
  • Changing credentials in the local config file didn't actually take effect until something else changed — the app kept using stale values. This affected Google sign-in settings too, not just analytics.

issues.display_title: Issue #184: Track which Edit tools are actually used
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

Description

Problem: The Edit page has 15 tools, and we have no idea which ones people actually use. We can't tell which tools deserve more attention, which ones are being ignored, or whether a newly shipped tool ever got picked up. Right now the only usage data we collect covers file browsing and uploads — nothing from Edit at all.

Solution: Report a "generate" every time a user starts a job in Edit, tagged with which tool it was.

Tools covered:

  • Nadir Builder
  • AI Nadir Patching (Remove Tripod)
  • Logo Nadir Patching (Add Logo)
  • Enfuse
  • Cube to Equirectangular
  • Equirectangular to Cube
  • Batch Image Resize
  • Image Minifier
  • 360 Image Leveling (Straighten)
  • Crop Image
  • Virtual Stage 360 Images
  • 2D Virtual Stage
  • Scale Up Image
  • Stitch 360 Panorama

Not covered: Image to Video — the feature isn't released yet, so there's nothing to measure.

What gets reported: only the name of the tool. No file names, no folder paths, no settings, no image contents.

Behavior:

  • Counted once per run, when the job starts — not once per photo. Running a batch of 100 photos counts as one use, same as running a single photo.
  • Re-running a failed item counts as a new use, since it does start real work again.
  • Not counted if the run never actually starts (empty queue, no output folder picked, or the user backs out of the overwrite warning).
  • Only released builds report; local development runs stay silent.

issues.display_title: Issue #176: First-time intro when entering the Stitching page
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

Description

Problem: New users who haven't used Stitching before don't know where to start — what kind of photos to prepare, how many, or what the end result looks like.

Solution: The first time a user opens the Stitching page, a short intro pop-up appears with:

  • A welcome title + brief explanation of how the feature works (take 4 photos from one spot with a panoramic head, add them to the queue, they get combined into one 360° panorama).
  • Visual examples: the 4 sample input photos, and the resulting panorama photo.
  • A "Got it" button to dismiss.

Behavior:

  • Only shows automatically once (won't keep forcing itself on the same device/browser).
  • Can still be reopened anytime via a "Replay intro" button in the help (FAQ) panel on the right side of the Stitching page.

Shipped in #175.

issues.display_title: Issue #177: First-time intro when entering the Manual Control Points page
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

Description

Problem: "Manual control points" is used to fix a panorama seam that came out wrong (e.g. a visible tear/line). But the interaction — clicking the same feature in two different photos — is hard to explain in words, and previously there was only a single small hint line at the bottom of the modal.

Solution: The first time a user opens the "Manual control points" modal, a pop-up appears with:

  • A title + a short looping video demonstrating how to click the same feature in photo A, then the matching spot in photo B.
  • Numbered steps: pick a seam from the list → click the same feature in both photos → repeat for at least a few points per seam → save.
  • A "Got it" button to dismiss.

Behavior:

  • Only shows automatically once.
  • Can be reopened via an icon button at the top of the modal, next to the Undo button.

Shipped in #175.

issues.display_title: Issue #178: Warning and layout fix when fewer than 4 photos are selected
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

Description

Problem: A panorama group ideally needs 4 photos (from 4 directions at one spot). When a user added only 1 photo, the group card looked broken — the single photo stretched to fill the entire card, reading like a rendering glitch rather than "this group just isn't finished yet." When 2-3 photos were added, the warning message was also unclear.

Solution:

  • The panorama card now always shows 4 photo slots, even when the group isn't complete yet — empty slots show a dashed placeholder icon instead of the layout collapsing to one oversized tile.
  • The warning message is now direct: it simply says "a panorama needs 4 photos" instead of ambiguous wording like "needs at least 2" or "needs 4 or more," which left it unclear how many photos were actually required.
  • This message has also been translated, so it now displays correctly in every language the app supports (previously it only existed in English).

Shipped in #175.

issues.display_title: Issue #173: Implement 2D Object Remover in Edit
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

Description

Problem: Getting rid of something you don't want in a photo — a stray bin, a parked car, a person walking through the shot, a sign — means leaving the app entirely and doing it in Photoshop or an online editor. For a photographer working through a folder of listing photos that is a lot of back and forth, and the app can't help with any of it.

Solution: A new Edit tool that removes objects from ordinary flat photos. Mark what you want gone, and AI rebuilds what should be behind it.

How marking works: two ways, and they can be mixed on the same photo.

  • Box — drag a rectangle around the object. Fast, good for something standing on its own.
  • Brush — trace over the object. Slower, but a rectangle drawn around an object in a crowded scene always takes its neighbours with it, and the brush follows the actual shape instead.

Each mark can be given a name ("bin", "car") to tell the AI what it is looking at, and can be reselected, moved, resized or deleted before you run it.

Behavior:

  • The tool only accepts standard flat photos. Dropping a 360° panorama shows a message pointing to the 360 version of this tool instead.
  • Save as new file ON writes the result to an Object remover folder next to the original, leaving the original untouched. OFF replaces the original — with a confirmation prompt first, so nobody overwrites a photo by accident.
  • The result appears in a before/after slider so the change can be judged against the original.
  • Everything outside the marks is kept as it was. Both AI providers re-render the whole frame rather than editing only the marked patch, so furniture, paperwork and table edges nowhere near the target used to come back subtly redrawn — the finished image now takes those pixels from the source photo.
  • Needs an AI API key (added under Preferences). The Remove button stays disabled until a valid key exists, so the failure is visible up front rather than after a long wait.

Shipped in #185.

issues.display_title: Issue #174: Implement 360 Object Remover in Edit
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

2026-08-14.20-09-46.mp4

Problem: The same unwanted-object problem as #173, but for 360° panoramas — and there the usual tools are worse. A panorama opened in a normal photo editor looks stretched and distorted at the top and bottom, the left and right edges have to line up seamlessly or the sphere visibly breaks, and most AI tools hand back something that no longer works as a 360 at all.

Solution: A 360 version of the Object Remover. Same marking, same result, but built so a panorama survives it.

Why it needs its own tool: a panorama can't just be handed to the AI whole — the projection stretches everything near the ceiling and floor, and the seam where the two edges meet gets broken. Instead the app takes each marked object as its own normal-looking view, cleans that view, and merges it back into the sphere. The user doesn't see any of this; they mark and press the button.

How marking works: identical to #173 — box or brush, mixed freely, each mark nameable and editable before running.

Behavior:

  • Only accepts 360° panoramas. Dropping a flat photo points to the 2D version instead.
  • Save as new file ON writes to a 360 Object remover folder next to the original. OFF replaces the original, with a confirmation prompt first.
  • The panorama stays a panorama. The hidden information that marks a file as 360° (which is what makes viewers and Street View show it as a sphere rather than a stretched rectangle) is carried over to the result, along with the camera details and date. Without this the output would silently stop being a usable panorama.
  • Each marked object is handled separately, so if one of them fails the rest still come through. When that happens the app says the result is partial instead of reporting a clean success, so nobody ships a panorama assuming everything was removed.
  • If every object fails, the original file is left completely untouched rather than being replaced by a pointless re-save.
  • Needs an AI API key, same as #173.

Shipped in #185.

issues.display_title: Issue #180: Add Delete button to the Unable to Load Files modal
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

Video.Project.17.mp4

Problem

When a file fails to load, the Unable to Load Files modal only offers Close and Reload. A file that is corrupt or permanently unreadable will keep failing on Reload, and the user has to close the dialog and hunt the file down in Browse to remove it.

Request

Add a Delete button to the load-error modal so the broken file can be removed straight from the dialog.

Scope

  • src/renderer/components/modals/MessageModal.tsx — optional file prop; render a danger Delete button only when a file is supplied.
  • Delete routes through the existing requestDelete flow (src/renderer/features/files/deleteConfirm.ts), so the confirm-before-delete preference / session skip behaves the same as the toolbar trash button.
  • Call sites pass the file that actually failed:
    • src/renderer/features/preview/Browse.tsx
    • src/renderer/components/features/Edit/Browse.tsx
    • src/renderer/features/preview/Main.tsx
  • src/renderer/features/preview/hooks/useViewerImage.ts — the viewer error path calls selectDisplayImg(null) before the modal opens, so displayedFile is already cleared; the failed file has to be captured in the modal state.

Acceptance criteria

  • Clicking a failed thumbnail in Browse (Preview and Edit) shows the modal with Delete, Close, Reload.
  • A viewer load failure shows the modal with Delete targeting the file that failed.
  • Delete honours the "confirm before deleting" preference and the session-skip checkbox.
  • After delete, the folder listing no longer shows the file.
  • Button label uses the existing t_delete key — no new i18n key.
